In article <4l9tp3$fnh@freenet-news.carleton.ca>,
bb748@FreeNet.Carleton.CA (Milton Kleim) wrote:

> INDUSTRIAL SOCIETY AND ITS FUTURE
> 
> By Theodore Kaczynski
> 
> 
>    INTRODUCTION
>    
>    1. The Industrial Revolution and its consequences have been a disaster
>    for the human race. They have greatly increased the life-expectancy of
>    those of us who live in "advanced" countries, but they have
>    destabilized society, have made life unfulfilling, have subjected
>    human beings to indignities, have led to widespread psychological
>    suffering (in the Third World to physical suffering as well) and have
>    inflicted severe damage on the natural world. The continued
>    development of technology will worsen the situation. It will certainly
>    subject human beings to greater indignities and inflict greater damage
>    on the natural world, it will probably lead to greater social
>    disruption and psychological suffering, and it may lead to increased
>    physical suffering even in "advanced" countries.


This starts poorly. Not only it is mainly obfuscation, but he states a
series of personal opinions as fact, not a particularly strong foundation
to build his case upon. To claim that our current condition of unhappiness
and angst is the direct result of the industrial revolution is to assume
that there was a happier time somewhere in our past. History says
otherwise. Would Dr. Kaczynski be as happy as a Russian peasant serf under
the Tzars, crippled by hard labor and dead at 35 from anthrax? Or as a
Zulu warrior (an agrarian hunter-gatherer society, stone-age technology)
where the murder rate was 10 times modern levels and the battles raged for
decades? Or be a medival peasant and get run through by a barbaian's blade
smeared with pig shit? In fact, to claim that the present level of the
world's fortunes is *lower* than it has been in the past is sheer
arrogance--it is insulting to the people of the past, who have *really*
suffered. All rhetoric aside, we live in a world where I can go from NY to
Peking to Moscow to Jersey and stay in a nearly-identical hotel, fly in
unimagined comfort, eat a nearly-identical hamburger at a nearly-identical
McDonalds, and not catch a life-threatening illness: and I can do this on
a studen'ts income, if I plan well. This is comfort in the extreme, and
the industrial revolution is its progenitor.

THE UNUCRITIC
